Learning Objectives
Recognize the effects of selecting an alternative arthroplasty option rather than conventional
total knee arthroplasty.
Specify surgical considerations in patients in whom an alternative arthroplasty option is
indicated.
Understand the anticipated clinical outcomes of alternative arthroplasty options.

Bicompartmental knee arthroplasty is a treatment option for the management of
osteoarthritis of the medial or lateral compartment and the patellofemoral compartment
(Resources 1 and 2).
Compared with conventional total knee arthroplasty (TKA), advantages include preservation of
bone stock, maintenance of knee kinematics, and retention of cruciate ligaments.
Disadvantages include increased technical demands of the procedure, risk of osteoarthritis
progression in the remaining compartment, unproven long-term survivorship, and lack of
established clinical benefit compared with TKA. In addition, the cost of two implants often
makes bicompartmental knee arthroplasty cost prohibitive for most facilities.

Overview
Osteoarthritis of the knee is a compartmental disease in which one, two, or all three
compartments of the knee may be diseased. Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA)
and patellofemoral arthroplasty (PFA) are commonly performed to manage
osteoarthritis in an isolated compartment of the knee. Typically, evidence of
osteoarthritis in a second compartment has been considered a contraindication to
isolated medial or lateral UKA or PFA. If a patient has osteoarthritis of the medial or
lateral compartment and the patellofemoral compartment, TKA is commonly performed;
however, bicompartmental knee arthroplasty is an alternative treatment option.
Osteoarthritis most commonly affects the medial compartment, with radiographic
progression migrating to the patellofemoral compartment, and the lateral compartment
frequently does not demonstrate radiographic evidence of disease progression.1,2
Approximately 28% of patients in the United States who undergo TKA have
bicompartmental osteoarthritis.3 Therefore, performing bicompartmental knee
arthroplasty to manage the medial and patellofemoral compartments rather than TKA
allows for preservation of bone stock in the lateral compartment, maintenance of knee
stability with retention of both cruciate ligaments, and maintenance of knee kinematics.
Deep flexion in the native knee occurs in concert with the ligaments, osseous anatomy of
the tibial plateau, and lateral meniscus compliance. The native knee undergoes rollback
with internal rotation the tibia pivoting on the medial tibial plateau.4 The rollback and
rotation of the tibia allows for the tibial plateau to avoid femoral impingement during

impingement to facilitate deep flexion.5 The mechanisms for this complex interaction to
allow for deep flexion are maintained only with preservation of both cruciate ligaments
and a healthy lateral compartment. Compared with TKA, which may result in alterations
in gait, including decreased ambulatory velocity and stride length and quadriceps
avoidance while climbing stairs, because of maintenance of the lateral compartment and
the cruciate ligaments, bicompartmental knee arthroplasty results in more normal gait
kinematics.6-9
Preoperative Evaluation
Patient history and physical examination are necessary to isolate the etiology of the complaint
and the pattern of arthritis and to determine the appropriate treatment option.
Preoperative radiographic evaluation should include weight-bearing AP, PA midflexion, lateral,
and Merchant views.

Preoperative Evaluation
Preoperative evaluation includes a thorough patient history to elicit the location of pain,
duration of symptoms, aggravating activities, previous treatments, and presence of
inflammatory arthritis. Physical examination must include evaluation of range of motion,
coronal alignment, ligamentous stability, and the presence of any fixed or correctable
deformities and evaluation of the ipsilateral hip. Radiographic evaluation should include
weight-bearing AP, PA flexion, lateral, and Merchant views (Figure 1).

The indications and contraindications for bicompartmental knee arthroplasty are similar
to those for UKA except for the additional presence of painful patellofemoral
osteoarthritis; however, several studies have shown that some patterns of
patellofemoral wear may be left unmanaged without compromising the results of medial
UKA.10,11 The indications and contraindications for bicompartmental knee arthroplasty
will continue to evolve alongside those for UKA, and bicompartmental knee arthroplasty
will most likely depend on the individual surgeon’s philosophy and experience regarding
management of the patellofemoral joint during UKA.

Surgical Technique and Implant Selection
Implants are available as monolithic or modular, unlinked options.
Monolithic implants are more technically challenging, are associated with higher rates of
revision surgery, and have been withdrawn from the market, except for custom
bicompartmental knee arthroplasty implants.
Modular, unlinked implants are associated with better long-term outcomes and lower rates of
revision surgery.

Surgical Technique and Implant Selection
The implants for bicompartmental knee arthroplasty are broadly grouped as monolithic
or modular, unlinked implant designs. Monolithic options included an off-the-shelf
design and a custom design. Off-the-shelf monolithic medial and patellofemoral
compartment arthroplasty implants were recalled because of high rates of pain and
patellar maltracking related to challenges in femoral implant sizing and positioning and
tibial baseplate fracture.12 The only current commercially available monolithic implant is
a custom implant with options to address the medial or lateral and patellofemoral
compartments. Monolithic implants are more technically challenging because of the
need to simultaneously align the trochlear and distal femoral condylar portions of the
implant.13 More commonly, because of unacceptably high rates of revision surgery and
the technical challenges associated with implantation of monolithic designs, modular,
unlinked UKA and PFA implants are being used for bicompartmental knee arthroplasty,
with independent resurfacing, alignment, sizing, and positioning of the medial or lateral
and patellofemoral components.12,14,15
Typically, a mini-medial parapatellar or midvastus approach is used for bicompartmental
knee arthroplasty to address the medial and patellofemoral compartments (Video 1). A
lateral parapatellar arthrotomy may be used for lateral bicompartmental knee
arthroplasty. The reduced amount of dissection and lack of tibia subluxation compared
with TKA is believed to decrease blood loss and provide a quicker recovery.16 The

Adjustments, such as downsizing of the femoral size of the UKA or PFA implants, may be

trochlear component is well tolerated and can be cleared of intervening articulating
cartilage. The primary disadvantages of unlinked UKA and PFA implants include
extended surgical time and the cumulative cost of two implants compared with a
primary TKA implant, which may render this approach for bicompartmental knee
arthritis economically unviable depending on negotiated implant costs.

Clinical and Functional Outcomes
Initially, monolithic bicompartmental knee arthroplasty resulted in poor outcomes, with high
rates of revision surgery for pain and patellar maltracking.
Modern unlinked implant designs are associated with improved survivorship and functional
outcomes.
Randomized clinical trials have shown no substantial differences in functional outcomes
compared with TKA.

Clinical and Functional Outcomes
Early reports of modular bicompartmental knee arthroplasty demonstrated a reliable
reduction in pain and improved function;17 however, long-term outcomes for
bicompartmental knee arthroplasty were not favorable, with only 54% survivorship at a
follow-up of 17 years in a series of 77 knees in which medial UKA and PFA was
performed, mostly because of trochlear failure in cementless designs.17 As modern
techniques and implant designs have improved implant fixation and reduced osteolysis
from polyethylene wear, the reported modes of failure have likely been addressed. In
the series by Parratte et al,17 no knees were revised for progression of osteoarthritis,
which may suggest that survivorship with modern implant designs may be more
comparable with that of conventional TKA.
In the original randomized clinical trial comparing 25 bicompartmental knee arthroplasty
procedures and 25 TKA procedures, no substantial differences in Knee Society Scores
(KSS), Oxford Knee Scores, walking speed, and patient satisfaction were reported during
2-year follow-up;18 however, the bicompartmental knee arthroplasty group experienced
more revision procedures secondary to fracture of the tibial baseplate in the monolithic
implant. In an evaluation of modular, unlinked bicompartmental knee arthroplasty,
Kamath et al19 presented a series of 29 knees with a minimum 2-year follow-up that
showed substantial improvement in KSS, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome
Scores, Medical Outcomes Study 12-Item Short Form scores, Western Ontario and
McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores, and range of motion. Yeo et al20
reported the 5-year outcomes of a randomized clinical trial comparing 26 modular

demonstrated reduced blood loss for bicompartmental knee arthroplasty but no
substantial difference regarding functional outcomes based on KSS, Oxford Knee Scores,
and Bartlett Knee Scores. Although the literature lacks long-term survivorship of modern
modular, unlinked bicompartmental knee arthroplasty implants, midterm outcomes are
promising, with 95% survivorship at 5.5 years.21
Based on current available evidence, modern modular, unlinked bicompartmental knee
arthroplasty does not seem to afford improved functional outcomes compared with TKA;
however, bicompartmental knee arthroplasty offers unique kinematic advantages
compared with TKA that make it an attractive treatment option in appropriate patients.
Before more broad acceptance of bicompartmental knee arthroplasty, long-term
survivorship and cost analysis are necessary to assess the practicality of the procedure.
Bicruciate-Retaining Knee Arthroplasty
Overview
Bicruciate-retaining knee arthroplasty (BiKA) affords the theoretic advantages of improved
knee kinematics compared with conventional TKA (Resource 3)
During intraoperative evaluation, only 55% of patients undergoing TKA have an intact anterior
cruciate ligament (ACL).
BiKA has failed to gain widespread adoption because of several limitations of the implant
design and technical challenges during the procedure.

Overview
Although TKA has been considered a successful treatment option for the management
of severe degenerative joint disease of the knee, approximately 20% of patients report
dissatisfaction with their outcome.22 Because patients undergoing TKA typically are
elderly with low physical demand, TKA components were designed for this specific
patient population. However, the demographics of patients undergoing TKA have
gradually shifted toward a younger population with higher physical demands. Currently,

most TKA components are designed to sacrifice one or both of the cruciate ligaments;
unless the anatomic landmarks are reproduced and the soft tissues are tensioned
appropriately, alteration in the kinematics of the knee may occur. Despite advances in
TKA component design, the native kinematics of the knee have not been replicated
through the TKA component design alone. In the absence of the ACL, the TKA
component design must include additional constraint that theoretically alters
kinematics. BiKA, in which the ACL is preserved, has been hypothesized to provide
advantages compared with conventional ACL-sacrificing designs. The reduced need for
constraint in the prosthesis and retention of the proprioceptive nerve fibers in the ACL
are believed to improve knee kinematics and potentially affect patient satisfaction.
Despite the theoretic advantages of ACL retention, BiKA has not achieved widespread
adoption because of several limitations. First, the implant requires an intact ACL;
however, in a systematic review and meta-analysis, Roussi et al23 reported that 79% of
patients who underwent TKA had an ACL present and only 55% of patients who
underwent TKA had an intact ACL based on intraoperative evaluation. Therefore, routine
use of BiKA would require backup instrumentation, require additional surgical time for
conversion to conventional TKA instrumentation, and place additional strain on a
hospital’s central sterilization department. Second, uncertainty exists regarding the
degree of proprioception provided by the ACL in knees with severe arthritis. For
example, the proprioception argument has been made in favor of the cruciate-retaining
design, but it has not proved to improve patient satisfaction compared with the
posterior-stabilized or ultra-congruent designs. Advocates for BiKA have cited the series
by Pritchett,24 which reported that patients who underwent staged bilateral TKA
preferred the knee with a BiKA implant compared with the contralateral posterior-
sparing knee implant, as evidence for bicruciate retention. However, Pritchett also
reported patients favoring a medial pivot knee implant over the contralateral posterior-
sparing knee implant, suggesting that bicruciate retention likely was not driving
improved patient satisfaction. Third, preparation of the proximal tibia requires retention
of a central bone island with the ACL insertion. In patients with disruption of the bone
island, surgeons must proceed with conversion to conventional TKA instrumentation or
fixation of the bone island. Fourth, retention of the ACL limits exposure to the lateral
aspect of the knee, which paradoxically makes balancing of the TKA implant more
technically demanding and limits the degree of anterior subluxation for implantation of

the tibial component. Last, the lack of prosthetic constraint because of ACL retention
and the potential for late ACL rupture raise concerns for delayed instability.
Surgical Considerations
Patients must have intact cruciate ligaments to undergo BiKA.
Relative contraindications include a varus or valgus deformity greater than 10°, flexion of less
than 90°, a flexion contracture greater than 10°, or a recurvatum deformity.

Surgical Considerations
The indications for BiKA are similar to those for conventional TKA except for requiring
intact cruciate ligaments, minimal deformity, and good range of motion. The indications
are similar in many respects to those for UKA or bicompartmental knee arthroplasty.
Although ACL deficiency is a definitive contraindication to BiKA, an ACL with partial
degeneration and concern for competency is a controversial contraindication. Given that
BiKA in patients with late ACL rupture may result in functional instability, caution is
warranted against performing BiKA in patients with partial ACL degeneration.25 Similar
to the contraindications regarding coronal and sagittal deformity for UKA, BiKA is
relatively contraindicated in patients with a varus or valgus deformity greater than 10°,
flexion of less than 90°, a flexion contracture greater than 10°, or a recurvatum
deformity.26
Clinical and Functional Outcomes
Short-term survivorship of BiKA is concerning compared with that of conventional TKA despite
perceived improvements in component design.

BiKA is associated with unacceptably high rates of revision surgery, leading to very
limited adoption relative to the more common cruciate-retaining and posterior-stabilized
designs.27 Because of the theoretic advantages of retaining the ACL, developments in
BiKA designs have continued. Despite improvements in BiKA design, a retrospective
comparison study presented concerning rates of early revision surgery in patients who
underwent BiKA compared with cruciate-retaining knee arthroplasty.28 Christensen et
al28 reported a 5% revision surgery rate for BiKA compared with a 1.3% revision surgery
rate for cruciate-retaining knee arthroplasty with minimum follow-up of 12 months. In
addition, the authors reported higher rates of radiolucent lines in patients who
underwent BiKA and no considerable differences in functional outcomes. Expanding on
the same BiKA cohort, Pelt et al29 presented 3-year revision-free survivorship in 88% of
patients who underwent BiKA, with tibial loosening, ACL impingement, and continued
pain as the most common reasons for revision surgery. The recent randomized clinical
trial comparing various outcomes between 25 BiKA procedures and 25 cruciate-retaining
knee arthroplasty procedures reported no substantial difference in radiostereometric
analysis or difference between preoperative and 2-year postoperative functional
outcomes.30 The authors noted that revision surgery was necessary in four patients who
underwent BiKA and no patients who underwent cruciate-retaining knee arthroplasty,
resulting in a recommendation against the routine use of BiKA.
Patellofemoral Knee Arthroplasty
Overview
Isolated patellofemoral arthritis is present in 10% of the population and predominantly affects
females.
PFA is an alternative treatment option to TKA for the management of isolated patellofemoral
arthritis.

Overview
Isolated patellofemoral arthritis is relatively rare compared with medial compartment
arthritis; however, approximately 10% of the population older than 40 years is affected

Preoperative Evaluation
Patient history and physical examination typically are reliable methods for identifying
characteristics and symptoms consistent with isolated patellofemoral arthritis.
During evaluation of the patient, alternative etiologies of anterior knee pain, such as patellar
tendinitis, quadriceps tendinitis, bursitis, or referred ipsilateral hip pain, should be considered.
Preoperative radiographic evaluation should include weight-bearing AP, PA flexion, lateral, and
Merchant views.
MRIs or arthroscopic images are useful imaging studies to assess the patellofemoral
compartment and rule out tibiofemoral disease.


Preoperative Evaluation
The patient history and physical examination are critical components of diagnosing
isolated patellofemoral arthritis and excluding other etiologies for a patient’s symptoms.
The patient history will determine the location of pain, duration of symptoms,
aggravating activities, previous treatments, and the presence of inflammatory arthritis or
previous trauma. Symptoms caused by isolated patellofemoral arthritis will be anterior
knee pain located retropatellar or immediately peripatellar. The pain should be present
only during descending and ascending stairs, kneeling, squatting, standing from a seated
position, or walking on a decline. If pain is present during ambulation on level ground,
more diffuse pathology should be considered. Patients also should be evaluated for
other etiologies of anterior knee pain, including patellar tendinitis, quadriceps tendinitis,
bursitis, or referred ipsilateral hip pain.
Physical examination must include evaluation of range of motion, coronal alignment,
ligamentous stability, and any fixed or correctable deformities. Specific evaluation of the
patellofemoral compartment includes assessment for the presence of the J-sign,
evaluation of patellar apprehension, measurement of the Q-angle, and evaluation of
reproducible symptoms via the patellar grind test. Evaluation of patellar tracking is
important because uncorrectable malalignment must be addressed before PFA. Physical
examination for alternative sources of pain includes palpation of the medial and lateral
joint line and evaluation of the ipsilateral hip.
Radiographic evaluation includes weight-bearing AP, PA flexion, lateral, and Merchant
views (Figure 3). Preoperative weight-bearing radiographs are necessary to assess for
medial or lateral compartment osteoarthritis. The lateral and Merchant views are used
to determine the presence of patellofemoral arthritis, patella alta or baja, trochlear
dysplasia, patellar tilt, or patellar subluxation. MRI can be used to evaluate the
patellofemoral cartilage if a patient’s history and physical examination findings are
consistent with patellofemoral symptoms. Because isolated PFA is not well tolerated in

Patient selection is a key factor to a successful outcome. The indications for PFA have
evolved, but the primary indication is isolated patellofemoral compartment
osteoarthritis or traumatic arthritis. Patients with isolated patellofemoral arthritis
secondary to anatomic dysplasia or trauma are ideal candidates for PFA because they
are believed to be less prone to arthritis in the medial or lateral compartments with
time. In addition, patients with Outerbridge grade IV chondromalacia of the lateral
patellar facet or trochlear groove but less than grade III chondromalacia of the medial
and lateral compartments are considered PFA candidates. A patient’s symptoms are an
important consideration. Pain must be isolated to the anterior knee with activities
loading the patellofemoral compartment. Patients must have correctable patellar
maltracking with a normal or correctable Q-angle. Last, no age limitation has been
implemented; however, caution should be exercised in patients younger than 30 years.
Contraindications to PFA include isolated medial patellar facet chondromalacia,
inflammatory arthritis, uncorrectable patellar malalignment, medial or lateral
compartment disease, and flexion contracture. If a patient presents with pain not
isolated to the anterior knee or pain provoked with weight-bearing activities on level
ground, the patient is not a candidate for PFA. Last, caution should be exercised in
offering PFA to patients with disproportionate pain or patients taking narcotics to
manage their knee pain.
Surgical Technique and Implant Selection
Understanding trochlear component geometry is critical to avoiding complications associated
with poor patellar tracking.
Inlay trochlear component designs cause component internal rotation relative to the AP axis of
the femur, resulting in early failure.

Onlay trochlear component designs reduce component malpositioning by referencing the AP
axis of the femur and removing anatomic variability.

Surgical Technique and Implant Selection
Early implant designs were associated with problems related to trochlear component
geometry. The radius of curvature in early designs did not always allow the implant to sit
flush with the anterior and distal femur, causing the trochlear implant to catch on the
patellar component in early flexion or cause a mechanical block to full extension.
Proximal extension of the implant on the anterior femur was limited in early designs,
causing the patellar component to transition from articulating on the anterior femur to
the trochlear implant. The most important improvement in trochlear component
geometry has been the transition from inlay to onlay designs. As the name implies, an
inlay trochlear component sits recessed in the trochlear groove with the component
edges flush with the surrounding cartilage. The implications of the inlay design mean
that the component must match the native trochlear inclination. The mean trochlear
inclination is 11° internally rotated in relation to the AP axis of the femur in a normal
knee and 9° internally rotated in a dysplastic trochlear knee, which results in poor
patellar tracking, catching, and instability if the inlay component matches the native
anatomy.33 The onlay trochlear component is designed to sit on the anterior femur
perpendicular to the AP axis of the femur, which eliminates anatomic variability of the
native knee.
Regardless of implant design, a mini-medial parapatellar or midvastus approach is
commonly used to attain exposure for bony preparation; however, some surgeons may
prefer a lateral parapatellar approach. All marginal osteophytes are removed to ensure
that the onlay trochlear implant is not overhanging medial-lateral, is not impinging on
the intercondylar notch, and is recessed approximately 1 mm from the adjacent articular
cartilage. The patella is then resurfaced in the same manner as that for TKA, with the
goal of restoring patellar thickness. Similar to TKA, the patellar component is positioned
medial, and a lateral patellar facetectomy can be performed to improve patellar tracking
and avoid lateral bony facet impingement. Because of the potential for unexpected
findings of cartilage wear in medial or lateral compartments, the surgeon should be

Clinical and Functional Outcomes
Inlay trochlear component designs are associated with higher rates of revision surgery and
secondary surgery compared with onlay trochlear component designs.
The most common reason for early failure of PFA is patellar instability, whereas late failure is
the result of progressive symptomatic tibiofemoral arthritis.
Onlay trochlear component designs are associated with better functional outcomes without
increased complication rates compared with conventional TKA.

Clinical and Functional Outcomes
The primary mode of early PFA failure is patellar instability; therefore, the most critical
factor for a successful outcome is patellar tracking. In published series of PFA outcomes,
the use of inlay trochlear components was associated with patellar maltracking ranging
from 17% to 36% compared with less than 1% for onlay trochlear components.34,35 The
Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry demonstrated
cumulative 5-year revision surgery rates higher than 20% for inlay trochlear components
and less than 10% for onlay trochlear components.35 Progression of tibiofemoral
arthritis is the predominant mode of late failure. In a series of 103 knees, 12% of patients
underwent revision surgery for progression of tibiofemoral arthritis at a mean follow-up
of 55 months.36 Similarly, Kooijman et al37 reported that 25% of patients underwent
additional procedures for the management of progression of tibiofemoral arthritis at 15-
year follow-up. Interestingly, patients in whom isolated patellofemoral arthritis
developed secondary to trochlear dysplasia were less likely to experience symptomatic
tibiofemoral arthritis compared with patients treated for isolated patellofemoral
osteoarthritis.35 Because of improvements in cement fixation, aseptic loosening is rare,
with a series reporting a 2% rate of aseptic loosening at 15-year follow-up.37 However,

Reliable improvements in pain and functional outcomes can be achieved in patients
appropriately indicated for PFA.39 In patients with isolated patellofemoral arthritis who
underwent PFA or TKA, a retrospective series reported similar KSS scores and pain relief;
however, the PFA cohort had higher activity scores at a mean follow-up of 2.5 years.40
More recently, in a randomized clinical trial of 100 patients who underwent PFA or TKA,
substantially better Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scores, Oxford Knee Scores,
Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form scores, and range of motion in the PFA
cohort at a follow-up of 6 months.41 However, at a follow-up of 2 years, the PFA cohort
only had substantially better Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scores and range
of motion, with no difference in other functional outcomes or complication rates. In a
meta-analysis of 28 studies investigating complications and rates of revision surgery
between PFA and TKA, Dy et al42 reported a substantially higher likelihood of secondary
surgery and revision surgery in patients who underwent PFA compared with TKA;
however, the comparison of TKA implants with onlay trochlear components alone
revealed no substantial differences in secondary surgery and revision surgery.
